1	"""TAPA: dataflow HLS framework for fast compilation and high-frequency FPGA accelerators."""
     2	
     3	module(name = "tapa")
     4	
     5	bazel_dep(name = "bazel_skylib", version = "1.9.0", dev_dependency = True)
     6	bazel_dep(name = "platforms", version = "1.0.0", dev_dependency = True)
     7	bazel_dep(name = "rules_cc", version = "0.2.18", dev_dependency = True)
     8	bazel_dep(name = "rules_rust", version = "0.69.0", dev_dependency = True)
     9	bazel_dep(name = "rules_pkg", version = "1.2.0", dev_dependency = True)
    10	
    11	# 2.0.0-rc3 generated launchers require sys._base_executable, which is absent
    12	# from the Python used by the Ubuntu 18.04 CI image. Load-bearing: the
    13	# tapa-llvm-project repo references @rules_python//python:defs.bzl.
    14	bazel_dep(name = "rules_python", version = "1.9.0", dev_dependency = True)
    15	bazel_dep(name = "rules_shell", version = "0.8.0", dev_dependency = True)
    16	bazel_dep(name = "rules_verilator", version = "0.3.2", dev_dependency = True)
    17	bazel_dep(name = "rules_verilog", version = "1.1.1", dev_dependency = True)
    18	bazel_dep(name = "toolchains_llvm", version = "1.7.0", dev_dependency = True)
    19	bazel_dep(name = "verilator", version = "5.044", dev_dependency = True)
    20	
    21	# 5.046.bcr.3 pulls rules_cc_autoconf through BCR bison/flex/m4. That helper
    22	# requires C++17 <filesystem>, which is unavailable in the Ubuntu 18.04 CI image.
    23	single_version_override(
    24	    module_name = "verilator",
    25	    version = "5.044",
    26	)
    27	
    28	http_archive = use_repo_rule("@bazel_tools//tools/build_defs/repo:http.bzl", "http_archive")
    29	
    30	http_archive(

1	name: Nightly Jobs
     2	
     3	on:
     4	  schedule:
     5	    - cron: "8 9 * * *" # 09:08 UTC / 23:08 UTC-10 / 02:08 PDT / 01:08 PST
     6	  workflow_dispatch:
     7	
     8	jobs:
     9	  bump-version:
    10	    name: Bump Version
    11	    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    12	
    13	    steps:
    14	      - name: Checkout myself
    15	        uses: actions/checkout@v4
    16	        with:
    17	          fetch-depth: 0 # Fetch all history for all branches and tags.
    18	          token: ${{ secrets.GH_PUSH_PAT }} # Push with PAT to trigger CI.
    19	
    20	      - name: Bump version
    21	        id: bump-version
    22	        run: |
    23	          # https://github.com/actions/checkout/tree/d632683dd7b4114ad314bca15554477dd762a938?tab=readme-ov-file#push-a-commit-using-the-built-in-token
    24	          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
    25	          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
    26	          .github/scripts/bump-version.sh
    27	          if git diff --quiet "${GITHUB_SHA}"; then
    28	            echo "is-updated=false" >>"${GITHUB_OUTPUT}"
    29	          else
    30	            git push --force origin HEAD:ci/next
    31	            echo "is-updated=true" >>"${GITHUB_OUTPUT}"
    32	          fi
    33	        env:
    34	          # Using UTC-10 to generate date so the new version includes all
    35	          # commits from that date for most US timezones.
    36	          TZ: Pacific/Honolulu

     9	def _vpp_xclbin_impl(ctx):
    10	    vpp = ctx.executable.vpp
    11	    xo = ctx.file.xo
    12	    target = ctx.attr.target
    13	    top_name = ctx.attr.top_name
    14	    platform_name = ctx.attr.platform_name
    15	    xclbin = ctx.actions.declare_file(
    16	        ctx.attr.xclbin or "{}.{}.{}.xclbin".format(
    17	            top_name,
    18	            platform_name,
    19	            target,
    20	        ),
    21	    )
    22	
    23	    vpp_cmd = [
    24	        "--link",
    25	        "--output",
    26	        xclbin.path,
    27	        "--kernel",
    28	        top_name,
    29	        "--platform",
    30	        platform_name,
    31	        "--target",
    32	        target,
    33	        "--connectivity.nk",
    34	        "{top_name}:1:{top_name}".format(top_name = top_name),
    35	        xo.path,
    36	    ]
    37	
    38	    if target == "hw_emu":
    39	        # Limit mt_level to reduce process count (mt_level=2 balances speed vs resources).
    40	        vpp_cmd += [
    41	            "--vivado.prop=fileset.sim_1.xsim.compile.xsc.mt_level=2",
    42	            "--vivado.prop=fileset.sim_1.xsim.elaborate.mt_level=2",
    43	            # Xilinx's bundled GCC may not know about multiarch system header
    44	            # paths (e.g., /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu for asm/types.h).
    45	            "--vivado.prop=fileset.sim_1.xsim.compile.xsc.more_options={--gcc_compile_options -I/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu}",
    46	            # -B/tmp/tapa-compat-relr/ ensures bundled ld finds RELR-stripped libs
    47	            # before elaborate.sh's LIBRARY_PATH changes take effect.
    48	            "--vivado.prop=fileset.sim_1.xsim.elaborate.xsc.more_options={--gcc_compile_options -I/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu --gcc_link_options -B/tmp/tapa-compat-relr/}",
    49	        ]
    50	
    51	    ctx.actions.run(
    52	        outputs = [xclbin],
    53	        inputs = [xo],
    54	        tools = [vpp],
    55	        executable = vpp,
    56	        arguments = vpp_cmd,
    57	        mnemonic = "VppLink",
    58	        resource_set = _resource_set,
    59	    )
    60	
    61	    return [DefaultInfo(files = depset([xclbin]))]

    63	def _resource_set(_os, _num_inputs):
    64	    return {"memory": 2000}  # MB

    82	            doc = "The top function name of the kernel.",

    85	            mandatory = True,

    99	def _xilinx_wrapper_impl(ctx):
   100	    output = ctx.actions.declare_file(ctx.attr.name)
   101	    tool_path = "{}/{}/{}".format(
   102	        ctx.attr.tool_path,
   103	        ctx.attr.tool,
   104	        ctx.attr.tool_version,
   105	    )
   106	    lines = [
   107	        "#!/bin/bash",
   108	        "set -e",
   109	        # Pass through when local tools are not installed (e.g., macOS with remote execution).
   110	        'if [ ! -d "{}" ]; then'.format(tool_path),
   111	        '  exec "$@"',
   112	        "fi",
   113	        # Create a temp dir with sh -> bash: Xilinx tools use bash-specific syntax internally.
   114	        '_TAPA_SH_DIR="$(mktemp -d)"',
   115	        'ln -sf "$(command -v bash)" "$_TAPA_SH_DIR/sh"',
   116	        'export PATH="$_TAPA_SH_DIR:$PATH"',
   117	        'trap \'rm -rf "$_TAPA_SH_DIR"\' EXIT',
   118	        "source {}/settings64.sh".format(tool_path),
   119	    ]
   120	    if ctx.attr.xrt:
   121	        lines.append("source {}".format(ctx.attr.xrt_setup))
   122	
   123	    # Re-prepend after sourcing settings64.sh so our sh/xsc wrappers stay first.
   124	    lines.append('export PATH="$_TAPA_SH_DIR:$PATH"')
   125	    lines.append("export HOME=/tmp")
   126	
   127	    # Add multiarch header/library paths for Xilinx's bundled GCC.
   128	    lines.append('export CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH="/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu${CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH:+:$CPLUS_INCLUDE_PATH}"')
   129	    lines.append('export C_INCLUDE_PATH="/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu${C_INCLUDE_PATH:+:$C_INCLUDE_PATH}"')
   130	
   131	    # Use LIBRARY_PATH (not explicit -L) so compat libs below take priority.
   132	    lines.append('export LIBRARY_PATH="/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu:/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu${LIBRARY_PATH:+:$LIBRARY_PATH}"')
   133	
   134	    # Bundled binutils-2.37 cannot handle RELR relocations (requires >= 2.38).
   135	    # Create RELR-stripped copies of affected system libs and prepend to LIBRARY_PATH.
   136	    lines.append('_TAPA_COMPAT="$(mktemp -d)"')
   137	    lines.append('trap \'rm -rf "$_TAPA_SH_DIR" "$_TAPA_COMPAT"\' EXIT')
   138	    lines.append('if readelf -S /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 2>/dev/null | grep -q "\\.relr\\.dyn"; then')
   139	    lines.append("  if command -v objcopy >/dev/null 2>&1; then")
   140	    lines.append("    for _lib in /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libm.so.6 /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libmvec.so.1; do")
   141	    lines.append('      if [ -f "$_lib" ] && readelf -S "$_lib" 2>/dev/null | grep -q "\\.relr\\.dyn"; then')
   142	    lines.append('        objcopy --remove-section .relr.dyn "$_lib" "$_TAPA_COMPAT/$(basename $_lib)"')
   143	    lines.append("      fi")
   144	    lines.append("    done")
   145	
   146	    # Linker script for libc.so pointing to stripped copies.
   147	    lines.append('    if [ -f "$_TAPA_COMPAT/libc.so.6" ]; then')
   148	    lines.append('      _ld_so="$_TAPA_COMPAT/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2"')
   149	    lines.append('      [ -f "$_ld_so" ] || _ld_so=/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2')
   150	    lines.append('      printf "OUTPUT_FORMAT(elf64-x86-64)\\nGROUP ( %s/libc.so.6 /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc_nonshared.a AS_NEEDED ( %s ) )\\n" "$_TAPA_COMPAT" "$_ld_so" > "$_TAPA_COMPAT/libc.so"')
   151	    lines.append("    fi")
   152	
   153	    # Linker script for libm.so pointing to stripped copies.
   154	    lines.append('    if [ -f "$_TAPA_COMPAT/libm.so.6" ]; then')
   155	    lines.append('      _mvec="$_TAPA_COMPAT/libmvec.so.1"')
   156	    lines.append('      [ -f "$_mvec" ] || _mvec=/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libmvec.so.1')
   157	    lines.append('      printf "OUTPUT_FORMAT(elf64-x86-64)\\nGROUP ( %s/libm.so.6 AS_NEEDED ( %s ) )\\n" "$_TAPA_COMPAT" "$_mvec" > "$_TAPA_COMPAT/libm.so"')
   158	    lines.append("    fi")
   159	    lines.append('    export LIBRARY_PATH="$_TAPA_COMPAT:$LIBRARY_PATH"')
   160	
   161	    # Populate /tmp/tapa-compat-relr/ for the -B flag in v++ elaborate xsc.more_options.
   162	    # elaborate.sh prepends /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu to LIBRARY_PATH, so -B is critical.
   163	    lines.append("    if [ ! -d /tmp/tapa-compat-relr ]; then")
   164	    lines.append('      cp -a "$_TAPA_COMPAT" /tmp/tapa-compat-relr.tmp.$$')
   165	
   166	    # Rewrite linker scripts to reference the final path instead of the tempdir.
   167	    lines.append('      sed -i "s|$_TAPA_COMPAT|/tmp/tapa-compat-relr|g" /tmp/tapa-compat-relr.tmp.$$/libc.so /tmp/tapa-compat-relr.tmp.$$/libm.so 2>/dev/null || true')
   168	    lines.append("      mv /tmp/tapa-compat-relr.tmp.$$ /tmp/tapa-compat-relr 2>/dev/null || rm -rf /tmp/tapa-compat-relr.tmp.$$")
   169	    lines.append("    fi")
   170	
   171	    # GCC specs file so bundled GCC always searches compat dir first.
   172	    # Needed because xelab calls bundled GCC with -B and PATH is not preserved.
   173	    lines.append('    _gcc_specs="$({gcc_dir}/bin/gcc -print-search-dirs 2>/dev/null | sed -n "s/install: //p")/specs"'.format(
   174	        gcc_dir = "{}/Vivado/{}/tps/lnx64/gcc-9.3.0".format(
   175	            ctx.attr.tool_path,
   176	            ctx.attr.tool_version,
   177	        ),
   178	    ))
   179	    lines.append('    if [ -n "$_gcc_specs" ] && [ ! -f "$_gcc_specs" ]; then')
   180	    lines.append('      printf "*self_spec:\\n-B/tmp/tapa-compat-relr/\\n" > "$_gcc_specs" 2>/dev/null || true')
   181	    lines.append("    fi")
   182	    lines.append("  fi")
   183	    lines.append("fi")
   184	    lines.append('export PLATFORM_REPO_PATHS="{}${{PLATFORM_REPO_PATHS:+:$PLATFORM_REPO_PATHS}}"'.format(
   185	        ctx.attr.platform_repo_paths,
   186	    ))
   187	    if ctx.attr.argv0:
   188	        lines.append('exec {} "$@"'.format(ctx.attr.argv0))
   189	    else:
   190	        lines.append('exec "$@"')
   191	    ctx.actions.write(output, "\n".join(lines), is_executable = True)
   192	    return [DefaultInfo(executable = output)]
   193	
   194	xilinx_wrapper = rule(
   195	    implementation = _xilinx_wrapper_impl,
   196	    executable = True,
   197	    attrs = {
   198	        "tool": attr.string(
   199	            mandatory = True,
   200	            doc = "The Xilinx tool under the tool path, e.g., Vivado, Vitis.",
   201	        ),
   202	        "argv0": attr.string(
   203	            doc = 'Optional "$0" prepended to "$@".',
   204	        ),
   205	        "xrt": attr.bool(
   206	            default = False,
   207	            doc = "If true, also set up XRT environment.",
   208	        ),
   209	        "xrt_setup": attr.string(
   210	            doc = "Path to XRT setup.sh script.",
   211	            default = XILINX_XRT_SETUP,
   212	        ),
   213	        "tool_path": attr.string(
   214	            doc = "The tool path for this target.",
   215	            default = XILINX_TOOL_PATH,
   216	        ),
   217	        "tool_version": attr.string(
   218	            doc = "The tool version for this target.",
   219	            default = XILINX_TOOL_VERSION,
   220	        ),
   221	        "platform_repo_paths": attr.string(
   222	            doc = "Colon-separated platform repository paths.",
   223	            default = XILINX_PLATFORM_REPO_PATHS,
   224	        ),
   225	    },
   226	)

1	# Building from Source
     2	
     3	```admonish note
     4	This guide is for **developers** contributing to or extending TAPA,
     5	or **advanced users** building TAPA from source for custom OS support.
     6	For FPGA accelerator development with TAPA, refer to the
     7	[User Documentation](../start/installation.md). This is also the recommended way to install
     8	TAPA for all users.
     9	```
    10	
    11	```admonish tip
    12	If your OS isn't officially supported, consider using a virtual machine
    13	or file a [feature request on GitHub](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/issues).
    14	```
    15	
    16	## System Prerequisites
    17	
    18	To build TAPA from source, you need:
    19	
    20	- [Bazel](https://bazel.build) 7.3.2 or later
    21	- [Binutils](https://www.gnu.org/software/binutils/) 2.30 or later
    22	- [Git](https://git-scm.com)
    23	- [Libstdc++](https://gcc.gnu.org/libstdc++/) matching the most recent GCC
    24	  version installed on your system
    25	- [Python](https://www.python.org) 3 or later for Bazel
    26	- [Other TAPA dependencies](../start/installation.md)
    27	
    28	Install these tools using your OS package manager. For Ubuntu:
    29	
    30	```bash
    31	# Install bazel
    32	sudo apt-get install apt-transport-https ca-certificates gnupg
    33	curl -fsSL https://bazel.build/bazel-release.pub.gpg \
    34	  | gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/bazel-archive-keyring.gpg
    35	echo "deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/bazel-archive-keyring.gpg] \
    36	    https://storage.googleapis.com/bazel-apt stable jdk1.8" \
    37	  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/bazel.list
    38	sudo apt-get install bazel
    39	
    40	# Install other tools
    41	sudo apt-get install binutils git python3
    42	```
    43	
    44	```admonish tip
    45	For Bazel installation on other OS, see the
    46	[Bazel documentation](https://docs.bazel.build/versions/main/install.html).
    47	```
    48	
    49	```admonish note
    50	The [Dockerfile in the TAPA repository](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/blob/main/.github/docker/build-env/Dockerfile.binary-dependencies)
    51	provides a complete build environment. Use it for containerized builds or
    52	run the Ubuntu commands to install required tools.
    53	```
    54	
    55	## Clone the Repository
    56	
    57	To get started with building TAPA from source, you'll need to clone the repository from GitHub:
    58	
    59	```bash
    60	git clone https://github.com/tuna/tapa.git
    61	```
    62	
    63	If you are contributing to TAPA, fork the repository and clone your fork
    64	instead. When you're ready to contribute, create a new branch for your
    65	changes, commit your work, and open a pull request to contribute your
    66	changes back to the main repository.
    67	
    68	## Modify the Build Configuration
    69	
    70	You may need to modify the `VARS.bzl` file in the repository's root directory
    71	to specify the correct Vivado installation paths and versions. The build script
    72	currently assumes default installation paths at
    73	`/opt/tools/xilinx/Vivado/2024.2` and
    74	`/opt/tools/xilinx/Vivado/2022.2` for Vivado, and
    75	`/opt/tools/xilinx/Vitis/2024.2` for Vitis.
    76	
    77	If your Xilinx tools are installed in non-standard locations, please modify
    78	the `XILINX_TOOL_PATH` variable to reference the correct base installation
    79	directory for your Vivado and Vitis installations. You should also update
    80	`XILINX_TOOL_VERSION` to specify the version of the latest Xilinx tools
    81	you have installed. With these settings properly configured, the system
    82	will expect your Vivado installation to be located at
    83	`{XILINX_TOOL_PATH}/Vivado/{XILINX_TOOL_VERSION}`.
    84	
    85	Furthermore, you should configure `XILINX_TOOL_LEGACY_VERSION` to indicate
    86	the earliest version of Xilinx tools installed on your system, along with
    87	`XILINX_TOOL_LEGACY_PATH` to point to the corresponding installation
    88	directory.
    89	
    90	If your system does not have the Xilinx Runtime (XRT) installed, you can
    91	modify the `HAS_XRT` variable in the `VARS.bzl` file to `False`. This
    92	will prevent the tests to fail due to the absence of XRT.
    93	
    94	## Build TAPA from Source
    95	
    96	To build TAPA, navigate to the root directory of the cloned repository and execute the following command:
    97	
    98	```bash
    99	bazel build //...
   100	```
   101	
   102	This command compiles all TAPA targets, including the compiler, runtime
   103	library, and tests.
   104	
   105	For building a specific target, replace `//...` with the desired target
   106	name. For instance, to build only the TAPA compiler:
   107	
   108	```bash
   109	bazel build //tapa-core:tapa
   110	```
   111	
   112	```admonish note
   113	To view all available targets, run `bazel query //...`.
   114	```
   115	
   116	To skip building for the tests, you could use:
   117	
   118	```bash
   119	bazel build //... -- -//tests/...
   120	```
   121	
   122	After the build process completes, you can find the compiled binaries in the
   123	`bazel-bin` directory. For example, the TAPA compiler binary is located at
   124	`bazel-bin/tapa-core/tapa`.
   125	
   126	```admonish note
   127	The build process duration may vary depending on your system's performance.
   128	LLVM, a significant dependency used by TAPA for code generation, requires
   129	considerable time to build. Bazel will cache it after the initial build.
   130	```
   131	
   132	## Use the Built TAPA
   133	
   134	```admonish important
   135	Remember to source the Vivado settings script before running the TAPA compiler.
   136	```
   137	
   138	Once TAPA is built, you can use the compiled TAPA compiler to compile your
   139	designs. For example:
   140	
   141	```bash
   142	bazel-bin/tapa-core/tapa compile \
   143	 -f tests/apps/bandwidth/bandwidth.cpp \
   144	 --cflags -Itests/apps/bandwidth/ \
   145	 -t Bandwidth \
   146	 --clock-period 3 \
   147	 --part-num xcu250-figd2104-2L-e
   148	```
   149	
   150	Remember to rerun the `bazel build` command whenever you make changes to the
   151	TAPA compiler or runtime library to ensure you're using the latest version.
   152	
   153	## Build the Documentation
   154	
   155	The documentation is written in Markdown and built with [mdBook](https://rust-lang.github.io/mdBook/). The Bazel build rules fetch the correct mdBook and mdbook-admonish binaries automatically — no separate install is needed.
   156	
   157	**Build a static HTML site:**
   158	
   159	```bash
   160	bazel build //docs:build
   161	```
   162	
   163	The output is a tarball at `bazel-bin/docs/book.tar.gz`. Extract it to browse the HTML locally.
   164	
   165	**Serve with live reload during editing:**
   166	
   167	```bash
   168	bazel run //docs:serve
   169	```
   170	
   171	This starts a local server (default: `http://localhost:3000`) that reloads automatically when source files change. Supported on Linux x86\_64, macOS x86\_64, and macOS arm64.
   172	
   173	```admonish note
   174	The documentation source lives under `docs/src/`. The Bazel targets handle mdbook-admonish preprocessing automatically; do not run `mdbook-admonish install` manually in the source tree.
   175	```
   176	
   177	## Run TAPA Tests
   178	
   179	To run all TAPA tests, including unit tests and integration tests, use the
   180	following command in the repository's root directory:
   181	
   182	```bash
   183	bazel test //...
   184	```
   185	
   186	For running a specific test, replace `//...` with the test name. For example,
   187	to test only a specific app:
   188	
   189	```bash
   190	bazel test //tests/apps/vadd:vadd-xosim
   191	```
   192	
   193	## Build Binary Distribution
   194	
   195	To create a binary distribution of TAPA, navigate to the root directory of the
   196	cloned repository and execute the following command:
   197	
   198	```bash
   199	bazel build --config=release //:tapa-pkg-tar
   200	```
   201	
   202	Find the generated binary distribution in the `bazel-bin` directory,
   203	as a tarball named `tapa-pkg-tar.tar`.
   204	
   205	## Install the Binary Distribution
   206	
   207	To install the binary distribution, extract the tarball to a directory of your
   208	choice:
   209	
   210	```bash
   211	tar -xvf bazel-bin/tapa-pkg-tar.tar -C /path/to/install
   212	```
   213	
   214	Access the TAPA compiler binary at `/path/to/install/usr/bin/tapa`.
   215	
   216	## Containerized Build (Advanced)
   217	
   218	For those who prefer a containerized build environment, TAPA offers a GitHub
   219	Actions workflow that can be run locally using `act`. This approach ensures
   220	a consistent build environment across different systems.
   221	
   222	### Prerequisites
   223	
   224	1. Install `act` by following the instructions in the
   225	   [act repository](https://nektosact.com).
   226	
   227	2. Ensure Docker is installed on your system, as `act` requires it to run
   228	   the workflow.
   229	
   230	### Configuration
   231	
   232	Before running `act`, set up the following configuration files:
   233	
   234	1. Create a `.secrets` file in the repository root with the following content:
   235	
   236	   ```text
   237	   UBUNTU_PRO_TOKEN=[YOUR_UBUNTU_PRO_TOKEN]
   238	   MAC_ADDRESS=de:ed:be:ef:ca:fe
   239	   ```
   240	
   241	   Replace `[YOUR_UBUNTU_PRO_TOKEN]` with your Ubuntu Pro token (available
   242	   free for personal use) and `de:ed:be:ef:ca:fe` with your Vivado license
   243	   MAC address.
   244	
   245	2. Update the `.actrc` file in the repository root:
   246	
   247	   ```text
   248	   --secret-file .secrets
   249	   ```
   250	
   251	3. If your Vivado license and installation locations differ from the defaults
   252	   (`/share/software/licenses/xilinx-ci.lic` and
   253	   `/share/software/tools` respectively), update
   254	   `.github/actions/run-docker/action.yml` accordingly.

    25	- [Python](https://www.python.org) 3 or later for Bazel
    26	- [Other TAPA dependencies](../start/installation.md)
    27	
    28	Install these tools using your OS package manager. For Ubuntu:
    29	
    30	```bash
    31	# Install bazel
    32	sudo apt-get install apt-transport-https ca-certificates gnupg
    33	curl -fsSL https://bazel.build/bazel-release.pub.gpg \
    34	  | gpg --dearmor | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/bazel-archive-keyring.gpg
    35	echo "deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/bazel-archive-keyring.gpg] \
    36	    https://storage.googleapis.com/bazel-apt stable jdk1.8" \
    37	  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/bazel.list
    38	sudo apt-get install bazel
    39	
    40	# Install other tools
    41	sudo apt-get install binutils git python3
    42	```
    43	
    44	```admonish tip
    45	For Bazel installation on other OS, see the
    46	[Bazel documentation](https://docs.bazel.build/versions/main/install.html).
    47	```
    48	
    49	```admonish note
    50	The [Dockerfile in the TAPA repository](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/blob/main/.github/docker/build-env/Dockerfile.binary-dependencies)
    51	provides a complete build environment. Use it for containerized builds or
    52	run the Ubuntu commands to install required tools.
    53	```
    54	
    55	## Clone the Repository
    56	
    57	To get started with building TAPA from source, you'll need to clone the repository from GitHub:
    58	
    59	```bash
    60	git clone https://github.com/tuna/tapa.git
    61	```
    62	
    63	If you are contributing to TAPA, fork the repository and clone your fork
    64	instead. When you're ready to contribute, create a new branch for your
    65	changes, commit your work, and open a pull request to contribute your
    66	changes back to the main repository.
    67	
    68	## Modify the Build Configuration
    69	
    70	You may need to modify the `VARS.bzl` file in the repository's root directory
    71	to specify the correct Vivado installation paths and versions. The build script
    72	currently assumes default installation paths at
    73	`/opt/tools/xilinx/Vivado/2024.2` and
    74	`/opt/tools/xilinx/Vivado/2022.2` for Vivado, and
    75	`/opt/tools/xilinx/Vitis/2024.2` for Vitis.
    76	
    77	If your Xilinx tools are installed in non-standard locations, please modify
    78	the `XILINX_TOOL_PATH` variable to reference the correct base installation
    79	directory for your Vivado and Vitis installations. You should also update
    80	`XILINX_TOOL_VERSION` to specify the version of the latest Xilinx tools
    81	you have installed. With these settings properly configured, the system
    82	will expect your Vivado installation to be located at
    83	`{XILINX_TOOL_PATH}/Vivado/{XILINX_TOOL_VERSION}`.
    84	
    85	Furthermore, you should configure `XILINX_TOOL_LEGACY_VERSION` to indicate
    86	the earliest version of Xilinx tools installed on your system, along with
    87	`XILINX_TOOL_LEGACY_PATH` to point to the corresponding installation
    88	directory.
    89	
    90	If your system does not have the Xilinx Runtime (XRT) installed, you can
    91	modify the `HAS_XRT` variable in the `VARS.bzl` file to `False`. This
    92	will prevent the tests to fail due to the absence of XRT.
    93	
    94	## Build TAPA from Source
    95	
    96	To build TAPA, navigate to the root directory of the cloned repository and execute the following command:
    97	
    98	```bash
    99	bazel build //...
   100	```
   101	
   102	This command compiles all TAPA targets, including the compiler, runtime
   103	library, and tests.
   104	
   105	For building a specific target, replace `//...` with the desired target
   106	name. For instance, to build only the TAPA compiler:
   107	
   108	```bash
   109	bazel build //tapa-core:tapa
   110	```
   111	
   112	```admonish note
   113	To view all available targets, run `bazel query //...`.
   114	```
   115	
   116	To skip building for the tests, you could use:
   117	
   118	```bash
   119	bazel build //... -- -//tests/...
   120	```
   121	
   122	After the build process completes, you can find the compiled binaries in the
   123	`bazel-bin` directory. For example, the TAPA compiler binary is located at
   124	`bazel-bin/tapa-core/tapa`.
   125	
   126	```admonish note
   127	The build process duration may vary depending on your system's performance.
   128	LLVM, a significant dependency used by TAPA for code generation, requires
   129	considerable time to build. Bazel will cache it after the initial build.
   130	```
   131	
   132	## Use the Built TAPA
   133	
   134	```admonish important
   135	Remember to source the Vivado settings script before running the TAPA compiler.
   136	```
   137	
   138	Once TAPA is built, you can use the compiled TAPA compiler to compile your
   139	designs. For example:
   140	
   141	```bash
   142	bazel-bin/tapa-core/tapa compile \
   143	 -f tests/apps/bandwidth/bandwidth.cpp \
   144	 --cflags -Itests/apps/bandwidth/ \
   145	 -t Bandwidth \
   146	 --clock-period 3 \
   147	 --part-num xcu250-figd2104-2L-e
   148	```
   149	
   150	Remember to rerun the `bazel build` command whenever you make changes to the
   151	TAPA compiler or runtime library to ensure you're using the latest version.
   152	
   153	## Build the Documentation
   154	
   155	The documentation is written in Markdown and built with [mdBook](https://rust-lang.github.io/mdBook/). The Bazel build rules fetch the correct mdBook and mdbook-admonish binaries automatically — no separate install is needed.
   156	
   157	**Build a static HTML site:**
   158	
   159	```bash
   160	bazel build //docs:build
   161	```
   162	
   163	The output is a tarball at `bazel-bin/docs/book.tar.gz`. Extract it to browse the HTML locally.
   164	
   165	**Serve with live reload during editing:**
   166	
   167	```bash
   168	bazel run //docs:serve
   169	```
   170	
   171	This starts a local server (default: `http://localhost:3000`) that reloads automatically when source files change. Supported on Linux x86\_64, macOS x86\_64, and macOS arm64.
   172	
   173	```admonish note
   174	The documentation source lives under `docs/src/`. The Bazel targets handle mdbook-admonish preprocessing automatically; do not run `mdbook-admonish install` manually in the source tree.
   175	```
   176	
   177	## Run TAPA Tests
   178	
   179	To run all TAPA tests, including unit tests and integration tests, use the
   180	following command in the repository's root directory:
   181	
   182	```bash
   183	bazel test //...
   184	```
   185	
   186	For running a specific test, replace `//...` with the test name. For example,
   187	to test only a specific app:
   188	
   189	```bash
   190	bazel test //tests/apps/vadd:vadd-xosim
   191	```
   192	
   193	## Build Binary Distribution
   194	
   195	To create a binary distribution of TAPA, navigate to the root directory of the
   196	cloned repository and execute the following command:
   197	
   198	```bash
   199	bazel build --config=release //:tapa-pkg-tar
   200	```
   201	
   202	Find the generated binary distribution in the `bazel-bin` directory,
   203	as a tarball named `tapa-pkg-tar.tar`.
   204	
   205	## Install the Binary Distribution
   206	
   207	To install the binary distribution, extract the tarball to a directory of your
   208	choice:
   209	
   210	```bash
   211	tar -xvf bazel-bin/tapa-pkg-tar.tar -C /path/to/install
   212	```
   213	
   214	Access the TAPA compiler binary at `/path/to/install/usr/bin/tapa`.
   215	
   216	## Containerized Build (Advanced)
   217	
   218	For those who prefer a containerized build environment, TAPA offers a GitHub
   219	Actions workflow that can be run locally using `act`. This approach ensures
   220	a consistent build environment across different systems.
   221	
   222	### Prerequisites
   223	
   224	1. Install `act` by following the instructions in the
   225	   [act repository](https://nektosact.com).
   226	
   227	2. Ensure Docker is installed on your system, as `act` requires it to run
   228	   the workflow.
   229	
   230	### Configuration
   231	
   232	Before running `act`, set up the following configuration files:
   233	
   234	1. Create a `.secrets` file in the repository root with the following content:
   235	
   236	   ```text
   237	   UBUNTU_PRO_TOKEN=[YOUR_UBUNTU_PRO_TOKEN]
   238	   MAC_ADDRESS=de:ed:be:ef:ca:fe
   239	   ```
   240	
   241	   Replace `[YOUR_UBUNTU_PRO_TOKEN]` with your Ubuntu Pro token (available
   242	   free for personal use) and `de:ed:be:ef:ca:fe` with your Vivado license

   244

    10	def _no_lto_transition_impl(settings, _attr):
    11	    """Remove LTO flags so deps produce regular ELF objects.
    12	
    13	    Xilinx's bundled linker (binutils-2.37) cannot handle LTO bitcode
    14	    objects produced by -flto=thin. This transition strips LTO flags from
    15	    the compilation so that static archives contain native ELF objects
    16	    that the old linker can process.
    17	    """
    18	    copts = [c for c in settings["//command_line_option:copt"] if "lto" not in c]
    19	    linkopts = [opt for opt in settings["//command_line_option:linkopt"] if "lto" not in opt]
    20	    return {
    21	        "//command_line_option:copt": copts,
    22	        "//command_line_option:linkopt": linkopts,
    23	    }
    24	
    25	_no_lto_transition = transition(
    26	    implementation = _no_lto_transition_impl,
    27	    inputs = ["//command_line_option:copt", "//command_line_option:linkopt"],
    28	    outputs = ["//command_line_option:copt", "//command_line_option:linkopt"],
    29	)

    32	    compile_options = [
    33	        "-Wall",
    34	        "-Werror",
    35	        "-Wno-sign-compare",
    36	        "-I/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu",  # multiarch headers for bundled GCC
    37	    ]

    39	    compile_options += ["-isystem" + x.path for x in ctx.files.includes]

# Baseline clippy policy for TAPA Rust code. `tools/test-tools` mirrors this
# table (kept in sync manually); `fpga-runtime` extends it with FFI-specific
# allows and a broader restriction-lint set — divergence from this baseline is
# intentional there, see fpga-runtime/Cargo.toml.
#
# Folding those two into this workspace to get one table looks obvious and was
# tried; both walls are load-bearing, so don't re-litigate without new facts:
#   - fpga-runtime: Cargo has no "inherit the workspace lints and add a few".
#     A package sets `lints.workspace = true` OR defines its own table, never
#     both — `cannot override 'workspace.lints' in 'lints'`. Merging would mean
#     either loosening this baseline for everyone (its FFI allows include
#     cast_possible_truncation) or copying its table into each of its crates.
#   - tools/test-tools: joining as an out-of-tree member works in Cargo (via
#     `package.workspace`), but //tools:test_tools builds through
#     `cargo_artifacts`, whose sandbox stages only that crate's own manifest +
#     sources. A member cannot resolve its workspace root from there, so the
#     merge trades a duplicated lint table for a broken or heavily coupled
#     Bazel build.
[workspace.lints.clippy]
# Enable lint groups
all = { level = "deny", priority = -1 }
pedantic = { level = "deny", priority = -1 }
nursery = { level = "deny", priority = -1 }

# Allow: adding doc sections to every fallible/panicking fn is too verbose
missing_errors_doc = "allow"
missing_panics_doc = "allow"

# Allow: const fn changes API semantics and is overzealous
missing_const_for_fn = "allow"

# Allow: common Rust module naming pattern
module_name_repetitions = "allow"

# Allow: option_if_let_else often less readable than match
option_if_let_else = "allow"

# Allow: too many trivial getters to annotate
must_use_candidate = "allow"

# Allow: cognitive complexity thresholds are too low for serde impls
cognitive_complexity = "allow"

# Allow: significant_drop_tightening has false positives
significant_drop_tightening = "allow"

# Allow: iteration order over HashMap/HashSet is irrelevant in schema crates
iter_over_hash_type = "allow"

# ── Restriction lints (cherry-picked) ──
# Style consistency
semicolon_outside_block = "deny"
needless_raw_strings = "deny"
missing_assert_message = "deny"

# Prevent common mistakes
dbg_macro = "deny"
todo = "deny"
unimplemented = "deny"
error_impl_error = "deny"
string_add = "deny"

# Prevent subtle bugs
assertions_on_result_states = "deny"
wildcard_enum_match_arm = "deny"

# Code quality

     2	
     3	def _parse_vars(contents):
     4	    vars = {}
     5	    for raw_line in contents.splitlines():
     6	        line = raw_line.strip()
     7	        if not line or line.startswith("#") or "=" not in line:
     8	            continue
     9	        name, value = [part.strip() for part in line.split("=", 1)]
    10	        if not name.isupper() or name.startswith("_"):
    11	            continue
    12	        vars[name] = value
    13	    return vars
    14	
    15	def _format_vars(vars):
    16	    return "\n".join(["{} = {}".format(key, vars[key]) for key in sorted(vars.keys())])
    17	
    18	def _vars_repository_impl(rctx):
    19	    """Repository rule that merges VARS.bzl with VARS.local.bzl overrides."""
    20	    defaults = rctx.path(rctx.attr.defaults)
    21	    local = rctx.path(str(defaults).replace("VARS.bzl", "VARS.local.bzl"))
    22	    merged = _parse_vars(rctx.read(defaults))
    23	    if local.exists:
    24	        merged.update(_parse_vars(rctx.read(local)))
    25	
    26	    rctx.file("vars.bzl", _format_vars(merged))
    27	    rctx.file("BUILD.bazel", "")
    28	
    29	_vars_repository = repository_rule(
    30	    implementation = _vars_repository_impl,
    31	    local = True,
    32	    attrs = {
    33	        "defaults": attr.label(
    34	            default = Label("//:VARS.bzl"),
    35	            allow_single_file = True,
    36	        ),
    37	    },
    38	)
    39	
    40	def _resolve_vars_impl(module_ctx):
    41	    _vars_repository(name = "vars")
    42	    return module_ctx.extension_metadata(
    43	        root_module_direct_deps = [],
    44	        root_module_direct_dev_deps = "all",
    45	        reproducible = False,
    46	    )
    47	
    48	resolve_vars = module_extension(
    49	    implementation = _resolve_vars_impl,
    50	)

1	# Runtime Flags
     2	
     3	This page covers environment variables and host executable flags that control TAPA behavior at runtime. These apply after compilation, during software simulation or fast hardware cosimulation.
     4	
     5	---
     6	
     7	## Environment Variables
     8	
     9	These variables are read by the host executable at startup.
    10	
    11	| Variable | Default | Description |
    12	|----------|---------|-------------|
    13	| `TAPA_CONCURRENCY` | Number of CPU cores | Number of parallel coroutine threads used by software simulation. Set to `1` for single-threaded, more reproducible simulation runs. Has no effect on HLS compilation parallelism (`-j`). |
    14	| `TAPA_STREAM_LOG_DIR` | (unset — logging disabled) | Directory for stream transfer logs. When set, TAPA writes one log file per named stream recording each value written to that stream. Useful for tracing data corruption during software simulation. |
    15	| `FRT_STREAM_DEBUG` | (unset) | When set, log every successful stream read and write in the DPI layer. Produces high-volume output; use only for targeted debugging. |
    16	| `FRT_COSIM_YIELD` | `1` (enabled) | When enabled, the DPI layer calls `thread::yield_now()` on empty reads or full writes. Disable with `0` to busy-wait instead. |
    17	| `FRT_XSIM_LEGACY` | `0` | Set to `1` to use the legacy xelab command-line format for older Vivado versions. |
    18	| `FRT_XOCL_BDF` | (unset) | PCIe Bus:Device:Function for XRT/OpenCL device selection. Equivalent to the `-xocl_bdf` gflag. |
    19	
    20	### Example: reproducible single-threaded simulation
    21	
    22	```bash
    23	TAPA_CONCURRENCY=1 ./vadd
    24	```
    25	
    26	### Example: enable stream logging
    27	
    28	```bash
    29	TAPA_STREAM_LOG_DIR=/tmp/stream-logs ./vadd
    30	```
    31	
    32	See [Software Simulation](../howto/software-simulation.md) for more on stream logging and debugging.
    33	
    34	---
    35	
    36	## Host Executable Flags (Fast Cosim)
    37	
    38	When the host executable is invoked with `--bitstream=vadd.xo`, it runs fast hardware cosimulation instead of software simulation. The following flags control cosim behavior. They are passed directly on the host executable command line.
    39	
    40	```admonish note
    41	These flags use single-dash prefix (e.g., `-cosim_work_dir`) because they are parsed by the host executable via gflags.
    42	```
    43	
    44	| Flag | Description |
    45	|------|-------------|
    46	| `-xsim_part_num <part>` | Target FPGA part number for simulation (e.g., `xcu280-fsvh2892-2L-e`). |
    47	| `-cosim_work_dir <dir>` | Persistent working directory for simulation artifacts. Without this flag, a temporary directory is used and deleted after the run. |
    48	| `-xsim_save_waveform` | Save simulation waveforms to a `.wdb` file in the work directory. Pair with `-cosim_work_dir`; without it, the temporary directory and all waveforms are deleted after the run. |
    49	| `-xsim_start_gui` | Open the Vivado GUI for interactive debugging during simulation. |
    50	| `-cosim_simulator <backend>` | Simulator backend: `xsim` (default, Linux only, requires Vivado) or `verilator` (cross-platform, no Vivado required). |
    51	| `-cosim_setup_only` | Run simulation setup only, then stop before executing the simulation. Useful for inspecting generated simulation files before committing to a full run. |
    52	| `-cosim_resume_from_post_sim` | Skip re-running the simulation and jump directly to post-simulation checks. Use after a completed simulation to re-run checks without re-simulating. |
    53	| `-cosim_work_dir_parallel` | Create a unique subdirectory per instance when running multiple concurrent simulations, preventing work directory collisions. |
    54	
    55	### Example: save waveforms from a named work directory
    56	
    57	```bash
    58	./vadd --bitstream vadd.xo \
    59	  -cosim_work_dir ./cosim_work \
    60	  -xsim_save_waveform \
    61	  1000
    62	```
    63	
    64	### Example: staged workflow (setup then resume)
    65	
    66	```bash
    67	# Step 1: set up and inspect the simulation environment
    68	./vadd --bitstream vadd.xo -cosim_work_dir ./cosim_work -cosim_setup_only 1000
    69	
    70	# Step 2: run post-simulation checks without re-simulating
    71	./vadd --bitstream vadd.xo -cosim_work_dir ./cosim_work -cosim_resume_from_post_sim 1000
    72	```
    73	
    74	For a full walkthrough of fast cosim workflows, see [Fast Hardware Simulation](../howto/fast-cosim.md).

1	# Runtime Flags
     2	
     3	This page covers environment variables and host executable flags that control TAPA behavior at runtime. These apply after compilation, during software simulation or fast hardware cosimulation.
     4	
     5	---
     6	
     7	## Environment Variables
     8	
     9	These variables are read by the host executable at startup.
    10	
    11	| Variable | Default | Description |
    12	|----------|---------|-------------|
    13	| `TAPA_CONCURRENCY` | Number of CPU cores | Number of parallel coroutine threads used by software simulation. Set to `1` for single-threaded, more reproducible simulation runs. Has no effect on HLS compilation parallelism (`-j`). |
    14	| `TAPA_STREAM_LOG_DIR` | (unset — logging disabled) | Directory for stream transfer logs. When set, TAPA writes one log file per named stream recording each value written to that stream. Useful for tracing data corruption during software simulation. |
    15	| `FRT_STREAM_DEBUG` | (unset) | When set, log every successful stream read and write in the DPI layer. Produces high-volume output; use only for targeted debugging. |
    16	| `FRT_COSIM_YIELD` | `1` (enabled) | When enabled, the DPI layer calls `thread::yield_now()` on empty reads or full writes. Disable with `0` to busy-wait instead. |
    17	| `FRT_XSIM_LEGACY` | `0` | Set to `1` to use the legacy xelab command-line format for older Vivado versions. |
    18	| `FRT_XOCL_BDF` | (unset) | PCIe Bus:Device:Function for XRT/OpenCL device selection. Equivalent to the `-xocl_bdf` gflag. |
    19	
    20	### Example: reproducible single-threaded simulation
    21	
    22	```bash
    23	TAPA_CONCURRENCY=1 ./vadd
    24	```
    25	
    26	### Example: enable stream logging
    27	
    28	```bash
    29	TAPA_STREAM_LOG_DIR=/tmp/stream-logs ./vadd
    30	```
    31	
    32	See [Software Simulation](../howto/software-simulation.md) for more on stream logging and debugging.
    33	
    34	---
    35	
    36	## Host Executable Flags (Fast Cosim)
    37	
    38	When the host executable is invoked with `--bitstream=vadd.xo`, it runs fast hardware cosimulation instead of software simulation. The following flags control cosim behavior. They are passed directly on the host executable command line.
    39	
    40	```admonish note
    41	These flags use single-dash prefix (e.g., `-cosim_work_dir`) because they are parsed by the host executable via gflags.
    42	```
    43	
    44	| Flag | Description |
    45	|------|-------------|
    46	| `-xsim_part_num <part>` | Target FPGA part number for simulation (e.g., `xcu280-fsvh2892-2L-e`). |
    47	| `-cosim_work_dir <dir>` | Persistent working directory for simulation artifacts. Without this flag, a temporary directory is used and deleted after the run. |
    48	| `-xsim_save_waveform` | Save simulation waveforms to a `.wdb` file in the work directory. Pair with `-cosim_work_dir`; without it, the temporary directory and all waveforms are deleted after the run. |
    49	| `-xsim_start_gui` | Open the Vivado GUI for interactive debugging during simulation. |
    50	| `-cosim_simulator <backend>` | Simulator backend: `xsim` (default, Linux only, requires Vivado) or `verilator` (cross-platform, no Vivado required). |
    51	| `-cosim_setup_only` | Run simulation setup only, then stop before executing the simulation. Useful for inspecting generated simulation files before committing to a full run. |
    52	| `-cosim_resume_from_post_sim` | Skip re-running the simulation and jump directly to post-simulation checks. Use after a completed simulation to re-run checks without re-simulating. |
    53	| `-cosim_work_dir_parallel` | Create a unique subdirectory per instance when running multiple concurrent simulations, preventing work directory collisions. |
    54	
    55	### Example: save waveforms from a named work directory
    56	
    57	```bash
    58	./vadd --bitstream vadd.xo \
    59	  -cosim_work_dir ./cosim_work \
    60	  -xsim_save_waveform \
    61	  1000
    62	```
    63	
    64	### Example: staged workflow (setup then resume)
    65	
    66	```bash

    68	./vadd --bitstream vadd.xo -cosim_work_dir ./cosim_work -cosim_setup_only 1000
    69	
    70	# Step 2: run post-simulation checks without re-simulating
    71	./vadd --bitstream vadd.xo -cosim_work_dir ./cosim_work -cosim_resume_from_post_sim 1000
    72	```
    73

1 6 7 # TAPA 8 9 [![Staging Build](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/actions/workflows/staging-build.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/actions/workflows/staging-build.yml) 10 [![Documentation](https://readthedocs.org/projects/tapa/badge/?version=latest)](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest) 11 12 TAPA is a task-parallel HLS framework that compiles C++ dataflow programs to Verilog RTL for Xilinx FPGAs. Software simulation runs on any Linux machine without FPGA hardware. 13 14 *C++ source → `tapa compile` → RTL (.xo) → Vitis v++ → FPGA bitstream* 15 16 TAPA is community maintained by the 17 [Tsinghua University TUNA Association](https://tuna.moe/). 18 19 Published results: 2× higher frequency on average versus Vivado 20 [[1]](https://doi.org/10.1145/3431920.3439289), with 7× faster compilation and 21 3× faster software simulation versus Vitis HLS 22 [[2]](https://doi.org/10.1109/fccm51124.2021.00032). 23 24 25 ## Quick Start 26 27 ### Install 28 29 ```bash 30 curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tuna/tapa/main/install.sh | sh -s -- -q 31 ``` 32 33 This installs the current **stable** release (0.1.20260319). With root 34 privileges, installs to `/opt/tapa` (symlinks in `/usr/local/bin`). Without 35 root, installs to `~/.tapa` and updates your shell `PATH`. 36 37 > **Note:** TAPA's internal toolchain is being incrementally refactored to Rust 38 > for improved performance and reliability. During this transition, we recommend 39 > staying on the stable release (`0.1.20260319`) for production workloads. To 40 > install the latest (potentially unstable) release instead, pass `--beta`: 41 > 42 > ```bash 43 > curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tuna/tapa/main/install.sh | sh -s -- -q --beta 44 > ``` 45 46 **Requirements:** Linux (Ubuntu 18.04+, Debian 10+, RHEL 9+, Fedora 34+, Amazon 47 Linux 2023), `g++` 7.5.0+. Vitis HLS 2022.1+ is required for RTL synthesis and 48 on-board execution — **not** for software simulation. 49 50 To install a specific version: 51 52 ```bash 53 curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tuna/tapa/main/install.sh \ 54 | TAPA_VERSION=0.1.20260319 sh -s -- -q 55 ``` 56 57 Releases: [github.com/tuna/tapa/releases](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/releases) 58 59 ### Software simulation (no FPGA required) 60 61 ```bash 62 # Compile kernel + host together using the tapa g++ wrapper 63 tapa g++ -- vadd.cpp vadd-host.cpp -o vadd 64 65 # Run — executes on the CPU using TAPA's coroutine simulator 66 ./vadd 67 ``` 68 69 Expected output: 70 ``` 71 I20000101 00:00:00.000000 0000000 task.h:66] running software simulation with TAPA library 72 kernel time: 1.19429 s 73 PASS! 74 ``` 75 76 ### Compile to hardware 77 78 ```bash 79 tapa compile \ 80 --top VecAdd \ 81 --part-num xcu280-fsvh2892-2L-e \ 82 --clock-period 3.33 \ 83 -f vadd.cpp \ 84 -o vadd.xo 85 86 # Run fast RTL cosimulation against the XO artifact 87 ./vadd --bitstream=vadd.xo 1000 88 ``` 89 90 91 ## Programming Model 92 93 A TAPA design is a directed graph of concurrent tasks connected by typed 94 streams. An upper-level task declares streams and launches child tasks; leaf 95 tasks perform computation. The same C++ code runs in software simulation and 96 compiles to RTL. 97 98 ```cpp 99 // Kernel file (vadd.cpp) 100 void VecAdd(tapa::mmap a, tapa::mmap b, 101 tapa::mmap c, uint64_t n) { 102 tapa::stream a_q("a"), b_q("b"), c_q("c"); 103 104 tapa::task() 105 .invoke(Mmap2Stream, a, n, a_q) // reads DRAM → stream 106 .invoke(Mmap2Stream, b, n, b_q) 107 .invoke(Add, a_q, b_q, c_q, n) // stream → stream 108 .invoke(Stream2Mmap, c_q, c, n); // stream → DRAM 109 } 110 111 // Host file (vadd-host.cpp) 112 tapa::invoke(VecAdd, FLAGS_bitstream, 113 tapa::read_only_mmap(a), 114 tapa::read_only_mmap(b), 115 tapa::write_only_mmap(c), n); 116 ``` 117 118 ## Documentation 119 120 Full documentation: **[tapa.readthedocs.io](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)** 121 122 | Section | Description | 123 |---------|-------------| 124 | [Installation](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/start/installation.html) | Install from release or build from source | 125 | [Your First Run](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/start/first-run.html) | Software simulation without FPGA hardware | 126 | [How-To Guides](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/howto/software-simulation.html) | Build, simulate, and deploy designs | 127 | [Tutorials](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/learning-path.html) | Annotated labs from vadd to floorplanning | 128 | [C++ API Reference](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/api.html) | Full API: tasks, streams, mmap, utilities | 129 | [CLI Reference](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/cli.html) | All `tapa` subcommands and flags | 130 | [Troubleshooting](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/troubleshoot/common-errors.html) | Common errors, deadlocks, cosim issues | 131 132 133 ## Building from Source 134 135 ```bash 136 # Install dependencies (Ubuntu/Debian) 137 sudo apt-get install g++ binutils git python3 138 139 # Install Bazel — see https://bazel.build/install 140 141 git clone https://github.com/tuna/tapa.git 142 cd tapa 143 bazel build //... 144 ``` 145 146 See [Building from Source](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/developer/build.html) for the full guide. 147 148 149 ## Published Results 150 151 - [Serpens](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3489517.3530420) (DAC'22): 270 MHz 152 on Xilinx Alveo U280 with 24 HBM channels; the Vitis HLS baseline failed to route. 153 - [Sextans](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3490422.3502357) (FPGA'22): 154 260 MHz on Xilinx Alveo U250 versus 189 MHz with Vivado baseline. 155 - [SPLAG](https://github.com/UCLA-VAST/splag) (FPGA'22): Up to 4.9× speedup 156 over prior FPGA accelerators; up to 0.9× vs. A100 GPU. 157 - [AutoSA](https://github.com/UCLA-VAST/AutoSA) (FPGA'21): Systolic-array compiler 158 with frequency improvements over Vitis HLS baseline. 159 - [Callipepla](https://github.com/UCLA-VAST/Callipepla) (FPGA'23): 3.94× speedup 160 over Xilinx XcgSolver; 3.34× better energy efficiency than A100 GPU. 161 - [LevelST](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3626202.3637568) (FPGA'24): 2.65× 162 speedup, 9.82× higher energy efficiency vs. V100/RTX 3060 with cuSPARSE. 163 - [CHIP-KNN](https://github.com/SFU-HiAccel/CHIP-KNN) (ICFPT'20 / TRETS'23): 164 252 MHz on Alveo U280 versus 165 MHz with Vivado; v2 up to 45× over 48-thread CPU. 165 166 167 ## Publications 168 169 Core papers describing the TAPA compiler and the physical design toolflow it integrates: 170 171 1. Yuze Chi et al. [Extending high-level synthesis for task-parallel programs](https://doi.org/10.1109/fccm51124.2021.00032). FCCM, 2021. 172 2. Licheng Guo et al. [TAPA: A scalable task-parallel dataflow programming framework for modern FPGAs with co-optimization of HLS and physical design](https://doi.org/10.1145/3609335). TRETS, 2023. 173 3. Licheng Guo et al. [AutoBridge: Coupling coarse-grained floorplanning and pipelining for high-frequency HLS design on multi-die FPGAs](https://doi.org/10.1145/3431920.3439289). FPGA, 2021. **(Best Paper Award)** 174 4. Young-kyu Choi et al. [TARO: Automatic optimization for free-running kernels in FPGA high-level synthesis](https://doi.org/10.1109/TCAD.2022.3216544). TCAD, 2022. 175 5. Licheng Guo et al. [RapidStream: Parallel physical implementation of FPGA HLS designs](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3490422.3502361). FPGA, 2022. **(Best Paper Award)** 176 6. Licheng Guo et al. [RapidStream 2.0: Automated parallel implementation of latency-insensitive FPGA designs through partial reconfiguration](https://doi.org/10.1145/3593025). TRETS, 2023. 177 7. Jason Lau et al. [RapidStream IR: Infrastructure for FPGA high-level physical synthesis](https://vast.cs.ucla.edu/sites/default/files/publications/522_Final_Manuscript.pdf). ICCAD, 2024. 178 8. Neha Prakriya et al. [TAPA-CS: Enabling scalable accelerator design on distributed HBM-FPGAs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.10189). ASPLOS, 2024. 179 9. Moazin Khatti et al. [PASTA: Programming and automation support for scalable task-parallel HLS programs on modern multi-die FPGAs](https://about.blaok.me/publication/fccm23-pasta/). FCCM, 2023 / TRETS, 2024. 180 10. Suhail Basalama, Jason Cong. [Stream-HLS: Towards automatic dataflow acceleration](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706628.3708878). FPGA, 2025. 181 11. Akhil Raj Baranwal, Zhenman Fang. [PoCo: Extending task-parallel HLS programming with shared multi-producer multi-consumer buffer support](https://www.sfu.ca/~zhenman/files/J22-TRETS2025-PoCo.pdf). TRETS, 2025. 182 183 For annotated descriptions and the full list of application papers, see [Publications](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/publications.html). 184 185 186 ## License 187 188 TAPA is open-source software licensed under the MIT license. 189 See [LICENSE](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/blob/main/LICENSE) for details. 190 191 192 --- 193 194 Copyright (c) 2026 TAPA community maintainers and contributors.

Without 35 root, installs to `~/.tapa` and updates your shell `PATH`. 36 37 > **Note:** TAPA's internal toolchain is being incrementally refactored to Rust 38 > for improved performance and reliability. During this transition, we recommend 39 > staying on the stable release (`0.1.20260319`) for production workloads. To 40 > install the latest (potentially unstable) release instead, pass `--beta`: 41 > 42 > ```bash 43 > curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tuna/tapa/main/install.sh | sh -s -- -q --beta 44 > ``` 45 46 **Requirements:** Linux (Ubuntu 18.04+, Debian 10+, RHEL 9+, Fedora 34+, Amazon 47 Linux 2023), `g++` 7.5.0+. Vitis HLS 2022.1+ is required for RTL synthesis and 48 on-board execution — **not** for software simulation. 49 50 To install a specific version: 51 52 ```bash 53 curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tuna/tapa/main/install.sh \ 54 | TAPA_VERSION=0.1.20260319 sh -s -- -q 55 ``` 56 57 Releases: [github.com/tuna/tapa/releases](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/releases) 58 59 ### Software simulation (no FPGA required) 60 61 ```bash 62 # Compile kernel + host together using the tapa g++ wrapper 63 tapa g++ -- vadd.cpp vadd-host.cpp -o vadd 64 65 # Run — executes on the CPU using TAPA's coroutine simulator 66 ./vadd 67 ``` 68 69 Expected output: 70 ``` 71 I20000101 00:00:00.000000 0000000 task.h:66] running software simulation with TAPA library 72 kernel time: 1.19429 s 73 PASS! 74 ``` 75 76 ### Compile to hardware 77 78 ```bash 79 tapa compile \ 80 --top VecAdd \ 81 --part-num xcu280-fsvh2892-2L-e \ 82 --clock-period 3.33 \ 83 -f vadd.cpp \ 84 -o vadd.xo 85 86 # Run fast RTL cosimulation against the XO artifact 87 ./vadd --bitstream=vadd.xo 1000 88 ``` 89 90 91 ## Programming Model 92 93 A TAPA design is a directed graph of concurrent tasks connected by typed 94 streams. An upper-level task declares streams and launches child tasks; leaf 95 tasks perform computation. The same C++ code runs in software simulation and 96 compiles to RTL. 97 98 ```cpp 99 // Kernel file (vadd.cpp) 100 void VecAdd(tapa::mmap a, tapa::mmap b, 101 tapa::mmap c, uint64_t n) { 102 tapa::stream a_q("a"), b_q("b"), c_q("c"); 103 104 tapa::task() 105 .invoke(Mmap2Stream, a, n, a_q) // reads DRAM → stream 106 .invoke(Mmap2Stream, b, n, b_q) 107 .invoke(Add, a_q, b_q, c_q, n) // stream → stream 108 .invoke(Stream2Mmap, c_q, c, n); // stream → DRAM 109 } 110 111 // Host file (vadd-host.cpp) 112 tapa::invoke(VecAdd, FLAGS_bitstream, 113 tapa::read_only_mmap(a), 114 tapa::read_only_mmap(b), 115 tapa::write_only_mmap(c), n); 116 ``` 117 118 ## Documentation 119 120 Full documentation: **[tapa.readthedocs.io](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)** 121 122 | Section | Description | 123 |---------|-------------| 124 | [Installation](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/start/installation.html) | Install from release or build from source | 125 | [Your First Run](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/start/first-run.html) | Software simulation without FPGA hardware | 126 | [How-To Guides](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/howto/software-simulation.html) | Build, simulate, and deploy designs | 127 | [Tutorials](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/learning-path.html) | Annotated labs from vadd to floorplanning | 128 | [C++ API Reference](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/api.html) | Full API: tasks, streams, mmap, utilities | 129 | [CLI Reference](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/cli.html) | All `tapa` subcommands and flags | 130 | [Troubleshooting](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/troubleshoot/common-errors.html) | Common errors, deadlocks, cosim issues | 131 132 133 ## Building from Source 134 135 ```bash 136 # Install dependencies (Ubuntu/Debian) 137 sudo apt-get install g++ binutils git python3 138 139 # Install Bazel — see https://bazel.build/install 140 141 git clone https://github.com/tuna/tapa.git 142 cd tapa 143 bazel build //... 144 ``` 145 146 See [Building from Source](https://tapa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/developer/build.html) for the full guide. 147 148 149 ## Published Results 150 151 - [Serpens](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3489517.3530420) (DAC'22): 270 MHz 152 on Xilinx Alveo U280 with 24 HBM channels; the Vitis HLS baseline failed to route. 153 - [Sextans](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3490422.3502357) (FPGA'22): 154 260 MHz on Xilinx Alveo U250 versus 189 MHz with Vivado baseline. 155 - [SPLAG](https://github.com/UCLA-VAST/splag) (FPGA'22): Up to 4.9× speedup 156 over prior FPGA accelerators; up to 0.9× vs. A100 GPU. 157 - [AutoSA](https://github.com/UCLA-VAST/AutoSA) (FPGA'21): Systolic-array compiler 158 with frequency improvements over Vitis HLS baseline. 159 - [Callipepla](https://github.com/UCLA-VAST/Callipepla) (FPGA'23): 3.94× speedup 160 over Xilinx XcgSolver; 3.34× better energy efficiency than A100 GPU. 161 - [LevelST](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3626202.3637568) (FPGA'24): 2.65× 162 speedup, 9.82× higher energy efficiency vs. V100/RTX 3060 with cuSPARSE. 163 - [CHIP-KNN](https://github.com/SFU-HiAccel/CHIP-KNN) (ICFPT'20 / TRETS'23): 164 252 MHz on Alveo U280 versus 165 MHz with Vivado; v2 up to 45× over 48-thread CPU. 165 166 167 ## Publications 168 169 Core papers describing the TAPA compiler and the physical design toolflow it integrates: 170 171 1. Yuze Chi et al. [Extending high-level synthesis for task-parallel programs](https://doi.org/10.1109/fccm51124.2021.00032). FCCM, 2021. 172 2. Licheng Guo et al. [TAPA: A scalable task-parallel dataflow programming framework for modern FPGAs with co-optimization of HLS and physical design](https://doi.org/10.1145/3609335). TRETS, 2023. 173 3. Licheng Guo et al. [AutoBridge: Coupling coarse-grained floorplanning and pipelining for high-frequency HLS design on multi-die FPGAs](https://doi.org/10.1145/3431920.3439289). FPGA, 2021. **(Best Paper Award)** 174 4. Young-kyu Choi et al. [TARO: Automatic optimization for free-running kernels in FPGA high-level synthesis](https://doi.org/10.1109/TCAD.2022.3216544). TCAD, 2022. 175 5. Licheng Guo et al. [RapidStream: Parallel physical implementation of FPGA HLS designs](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3490422.3502361). FPGA, 2022. **(Best Paper Award)** 176 6. Licheng Guo et al. [RapidStream 2.0: Automated parallel implementation of latency-insensitive FPGA designs through partial reconfiguration](https://doi.org/10.1145/3593025). TRETS, 2023. 177 7. Jason Lau et al. [RapidStream IR: Infrastructure for FPGA high-level physical synthesis](https://vast.cs.ucla.edu/sites/default/files/publications/522_Final_Manuscript.pdf). ICCAD, 2024. 178 8. 1	# Installation
     2	
     3	**Purpose:** Install TAPA on your development machine.
     4	
     5	**When to use this:** Setting up TAPA for the first time.
     6	
     7	## What you need
     8	
     9	| Dependency | Version | Notes |
    10	|------------|---------|-------|
    11	| GNU C++ Compiler (`g++`) | 7.5.0 or newer | Required for software simulation and deployment |
    12	| Xilinx Vitis | 2022.1 or newer | **Not needed for software simulation** — only required for RTL synthesis and deployment |
    13	
    14	TAPA has been tested on the following operating systems:
    15	
    16	| OS | Minimum version | Notes |
    17	|----|-----------------|-------|
    18	| Ubuntu | 18.04 | |
    19	| Debian | 10 | |
    20	| Red Hat Enterprise Linux | 9 | Derivatives (AlmaLinux 9+, Rocky Linux 9+) also supported |
    21	| Amazon Linux | 2023 | |
    22	| Fedora | 34 | Fedora 39+ may have minor issues due to C library changes and Vitis HLS incompatibility |
    23	
    24	## Install from release
    25	
    26	```bash
    27	curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tuna/tapa/main/install.sh | sh -s -- -q
    28	```
    29	
    30	This installs the current **stable** release (0.1.20260319). With root
    31	privileges, TAPA installs to `/opt/tapa` with symlinks in `/usr/local/bin`.
    32	Otherwise it installs to `~/.tapa` and adds itself to your `PATH` via your
    33	shell profile.
    34	
    35	```admonish info title="Rust migration in progress"
    36	TAPA's internal toolchain is being incrementally refactored to Rust for improved
    37	performance and reliability. During this transition, we recommend staying on the
    38	stable release (`0.1.20260319`) for production workloads. To try the latest
    39	(potentially unstable) release instead, pass `--beta`:
    40	
    41	    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tuna/tapa/main/install.sh | sh -s -- -q --beta
    42	```
    43	
    44	To install a specific version:
    45	
    46	```bash
    47	curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tuna/tapa/main/install.sh \
    48	  | TAPA_VERSION=0.1.20260319 sh -s -- -q
    49	```
    50	
    51	Releases are available at [github.com/tuna/tapa/releases](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/releases).
    52	
    53	## Install g++
    54	
    55	Install `g++` using the package manager for your OS.
    56	
    57	### Ubuntu / Debian
    58	
    59	For Ubuntu 18.04 and newer, or Debian 10 and newer:
    60	
    61	```bash
    62	sudo apt-get install g++
    63	```
    64	
    65	### RHEL / Amazon Linux
    66	
    67	For Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and newer, derivatives like AlmaLinux 9 and newer
    68	and Rocky Linux 9 and newer, or Amazon Linux 2023:
    69	
    70	```bash
    71	sudo yum install gcc-c++ libxcrypt-compat
    72	```
    73	
    74	### Fedora
    75	
    76	For Fedora 34 and newer. Fedora 39 and newer may have minor issues due to system
    77	C library changes and Vitis HLS tool incompatibility.
    78	
    79	```bash
    80	sudo yum install gcc-c++ libxcrypt-compat
    81	```
    82	
    83	## Verify installation
    84	
    85	```bash
    86	tapa --version
    87	```
    88	
    89	## Building from source
    90	
    91	For source builds (full toolchain requirements and build commands), see [Building from Source](../developer/build.md).
    92	
    93	```admonish warning
    94	If installation fails, see [Common Errors](../troubleshoot/common-errors.md) for known issues.
    95	```
    96	
    97	**Next step:** [Your First Run](first-run.md)

1	# Contributing to TAPA
     2	
     3	## Pull Request Process
     4	
     5	1. Fork the TAPA repository and create a new branch for your feature or bug fix.
     6	2. Ensure all tests pass and pre-commit hooks run successfully.
     7	3. Write a clear and concise description of your changes in the pull request.
     8	4. Request a review from the TAPA maintainers.
     9	
    10	### Continuous Integration
    11	
    12	TAPA uses GitHub Actions for continuous integration. The CI pipeline:
    13	
    14	1. Builds binary distributions on Ubuntu 18.04 self-hosted runners.
    15	2. Performs code quality checks using pre-commit hooks on every commit.
    16	3. Runs functional and integration tests via staging workflows across a matrix
    17	   of platforms and Vitis versions for every main branch push.
    18	
    19	### Documentation
    20	
    21	- Update the documentation in the `docs/` directory for any new features
    22	  or changes.
    23	- Use Markdown format for documentation files.
    24	- Run the following command in the `docs/` directory to build and preview
    25	  documentation changes locally:
    26	
    27	  ```bash
    28	  bash build.sh
    29	  ```
    30	
    31	### Testing
    32	
    33	- Add appropriate unit tests for new features or bug fixes.
    34	- Ensure all existing tests pass before submitting your changes.
    35	- Run the full test suite using the following command:
    36	
    37	  ```bash
    38	  bazel test //...
    39	  ```
    40	
    41	- If you change the task-graph schema, note that it has **two** implementations
    42	  that must agree: `tapacc/tapacc.cpp` emits the JSON, and the `tapa-ir` Rust
    43	  crate parses it with `deny_unknown_fields`. The fixtures under
    44	  `tapa-core/testdata/` are hand-written and cannot catch the two drifting
    45	  apart. `//tapa-core:tapacc_conformance_test` is what does: it runs the real
    46	  `tapacc` on `tests/apps/vadd/vadd.cpp` and strict-parses its verbatim
    47	  stdout. `tapacc` is a Clang tool that only builds on Linux, so the test is
    48	  gated on `@platforms//os:linux` and is skipped everywhere else:
    49	
    50	  ```bash
    51	  bazel test //tapa-core:tapacc_conformance_test  # Linux only
    52	  ```
    53	
    54	## Reporting Issues
    55	
    56	- Use the GitHub issue tracker to report bugs or suggest new features.
    57	- Provide a clear and concise description of the issue or feature request.
    58	- Include steps to reproduce the issue, if applicable.
    59	- Attach relevant log files or screenshots, if available.
    60	
    61	## Community Guidelines
    62	
    63	- Be respectful and considerate in all interactions with other contributors.
    64	- Provide constructive feedback on pull requests and issues.

1	# Full FPGA Compilation
     2	
     3	Compile a TAPA design to an FPGA bitstream and run it on hardware.
     4	
     5	## When to use this
     6	
     7	Use this guide after software simulation passes (see [Your First Run](first-run.md))
     8	and you are ready to target real hardware or run a more accurate RTL-level
     9	simulation.
    10	
    11	## What you need
    12	
    13	- TAPA installed — see [Installation](installation.md)
    14	- Xilinx Vitis 2022.1 or newer
    15	- A compatible Alveo platform (the examples below use the U250)
    16	- The vadd source files: [`vadd.cpp`](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/blob/main/tests/apps/vadd/vadd.cpp) and [`vadd-host.cpp`](https://github.com/tuna/tapa/blob/main/tests/apps/vadd/vadd-host.cpp)
    17	
    18	## Stage 1 — Synthesize to RTL
    19	
    20	Run `tapa compile` to translate the C++ kernel into an RTL object (`.xo`):
    21	
    22	```bash
    23	tapa \
    24	  compile \
    25	  --top VecAdd \
    26	  --part-num xcu250-figd2104-2L-e \
    27	  --clock-period 3.33 \
    28	  -f vadd.cpp \
    29	  -o vecadd.xo
    30	```
    31	
    32	| Flag | Meaning |
    33	|---|---|
    34	| `--top` | Name of the top-level TAPA task |
    35	| `--part-num` | Target FPGA part number |
    36	| `--clock-period` | Target clock period in nanoseconds |
    37	| `-f` | Kernel source file |
    38	| `-o` | Output XO file |
    39	
    40	```admonish note
    41	You can replace `--part-num` and `--clock-period` with `--platform` to
    42	target a Vitis platform directly, for example:
    43	
    44	    --platform xilinx_u250_gen3x16_xdma_4_1_202210_1
    45	
    46	HLS reports are written to `work.out/report/` after synthesis completes.
    47	```
    48	
    49	Artifact produced: `vecadd.xo`
    50	
    51	## Stage 2 — Fast hardware simulation
    52	
    53	Before waiting hours for a full bitstream, validate the RTL with TAPA's
    54	fast cosimulation. Pass the `.xo` file as the `--bitstream` argument:
    55	
    56	```bash
    57	./vadd --bitstream=vecadd.xo 1000
    58	```
    59	
    60	Fast cosim uses simplified models for external components (DRAM, AXI
    61	interconnect) so setup takes only a few seconds instead of the ten-plus
    62	minutes that Vitis cosimulation requires. A successful run prints `PASS!`.
    63	
    64	```admonish note
    65	The default simulator backend is `xsim`, which requires Vivado on Linux. To use
    66	Verilator instead (cross-platform, no Vivado required), pass `-cosim_simulator verilator`
    67	to the host executable: `./vadd --bitstream=vadd.xo -cosim_simulator verilator`.
    68	```
    69	
    70	## Stage 3 — Link to xclbin
    71	
    72	Use Vitis `v++` to link the `.xo` into a hardware bitstream. This step does
    73	not involve TAPA and typically takes several hours:
    74	
    75	```bash
    76	v++ -o vadd.xilinx_u250_gen3x16_xdma_4_1_202210_1.hw.xclbin \
    77	  --link \
    78	  --target hw \
    79	  --kernel VecAdd \
    80	  --platform xilinx_u250_gen3x16_xdma_4_1_202210_1 \
    81	  vecadd.xo
    82	```
    83	
    84	Artifact produced: `vadd.xilinx_u250_gen3x16_xdma_4_1_202210_1.hw.xclbin`
    85	
    86	```admonish warning
    87	Hardware binary generation typically takes several hours. Plan accordingly,
    88	and ensure your machine will remain available for the full duration.
    89	```
    90	
    91	## Stage 4 — On-board execution
    92	
    93	With an Alveo card installed and XRT configured, run the host binary and
    94	point it at the generated xclbin:
    95	
    96	```bash
    97	./vadd --bitstream=vadd.xilinx_u250_gen3x16_xdma_4_1_202210_1.hw.xclbin
    98	```
    99	
   100	A successful on-board run prints `PASS!`, confirming the accelerator
   101	produced correct results on real hardware.
   102	
   103	## Next step
   104	
   105	[The Programming Model](../concepts/programming-model.md)

1	# Cosimulation Issues
     2	
     3	**When to use this page:** When `--bitstream=vadd.xo` (fast cosim) runs differently from software simulation, or when cosim produces xsim or Verilator errors.
     4	
     5	---
     6	
     7	## Fast cosim vs software simulation mismatches
     8	
     9	If fast cosim fails (`FAIL!` or hangs) but software simulation passes, the most common causes are:
    10	
    11	- **Non-deterministic scheduling can expose races not visible in software simulation.** Software simulation uses coroutine scheduling that runs tasks cooperatively; RTL runs tasks truly in parallel. Races that are hidden by cooperative scheduling in software simulation may surface as failures in fast cosim. Fix: remove any assumptions about task ordering that are not enforced by stream synchronization.
    12	
    13	- **Blocking `async_mmap` operations inside pipelined loops.** A blocking call inside a pipelined loop can stall the pipeline in RTL in ways that software simulation does not model. Fix: use non-blocking reads/writes and manually handle the response FIFOs, or switch to `tapa::mmap` to simplify the memory access model while debugging.
    14	
    15	- **Non-deterministic task scheduling.** Software simulation uses coroutine scheduling that may resolve races differently than RTL. If results depend on the relative timing of two tasks, they may differ between simulation and RTL.
    16	
    17	```admonish note
    18	Fast cosim models DRAM with a simplified functional model. Throughput and latency numbers from fast cosim are not representative of on-board performance. Use fast cosim only to verify functional correctness.
    19	```
    20	
    21	---
    22	
    23	## HBM cross-channel access limitation
    24	
    25	```admonish warning
    26	Fast cosimulation does not support cross-channel access for HBM. Each AXI interface can only access one HBM channel. Designs that require cross-channel HBM access must be validated on hardware rather than in fast cosim.
    27	```
    28	
    29	If your design uses multiple HBM pseudo-channels and the fast cosim result does not match software simulation, verify that no single AXI port accesses more than one HBM channel.
    30	
    31	---
    32	
    33	## xsim issues
    34	
    35	### `xsim not found` or `Vivado not found`
    36	
    37	xsim is part of the Vivado installation. Source the Vivado environment script before running cosim:
    38	
    39	```bash
    40	source /opt/Xilinx/Vivado/2022.1/settings64.sh
    41	./vadd --bitstream=vadd.xo ...
    42	```
    43	
    44	Adjust the path to match your Vivado installation and version.
    45	
    46	### `xsim hangs at elaboration`
    47	
    48	Check that the `.xo` file was produced by a successful `tapa compile` run. A partial or corrupt `.xo` (from a failed or interrupted compilation) can cause elaboration to hang silently. Re-run `tapa compile` from scratch and verify it exits with status 0 before running cosim.
    49	
    50	### Segfault inside xsim
    51	
    52	This is typically a Vivado bug. Try switching to a different Vitis/Vivado version. Versions tested by the TAPA CI pipeline are listed in the TAPA repository's CI configuration.
    53	
    54	---
    55	
    56	## Verilator issues
    57	
    58	### `verilator not found`
    59	
    60	Install Verilator from your package manager or build from source:
    61	
    62	```bash
    63	# Debian/Ubuntu
    64	sudo apt install verilator
    65	```
    66	
    67	### Verilator compilation error (Verilog parsing error)
    68	
    69	TAPA generates Verilog targeting recent Verilator versions. If you see Verilog parsing errors, update Verilator to the version used in TAPA's CI pipeline.
    70	
    71	### No waveform support with Verilator
    72	
    73	Verilator simulation does not support waveform capture via the Vivado GUI. If you need waveform debugging, use xsim and pass `-xsim_save_waveform` as described below.
    74	
    75	---
    76	
    77	## Cosim produces wrong output (`FAIL!`) but xsim does not hang
    78	
    79	Run with waveform capture and a persistent work directory so you can inspect the simulation after it completes:
    80	
    81	```bash
    82	./vadd --bitstream=vadd.xo \
    83	  -cosim_work_dir ./cosim_work \
    84	  -xsim_save_waveform \
    85	  1000
    86	```
    87	
    88	Then open the waveform in Vivado GUI:
    89	
    90	```bash
    91	vivado -mode gui -source ./cosim_work/output/run/run_cosim.tcl
    92	```
    93	
    94	In the waveform viewer, add the AXI memory interface signals and compare the expected vs actual data on each transaction. Look for read data that does not match what the host wrote, or write transactions that target unexpected addresses.
    95	
    96	---
    97	
    98	## Stream diagnostics
    99	
   100	The DPI runtime reports stream progress periodically when a stream stalls (empty on read or full on write). These messages appear on stderr and include the port name and queue state:
   101	
   102	```
   103	frt-dpi: progress[a_fifo_s]: read_ok=16 read_empty=40M write_ok=0 write_full=0 q_head=8 q_tail=8
   104	```
   105	
   106	| Field | Meaning |
   107	|-------|---------|
   108	| `progress[port]` | The port that triggered the report (the one currently stalling). |
   109	| `read_ok` | Total successful reads across all ports in this process. |
   110	| `read_empty` | Total empty-read attempts (queue had no data). |
   111	| `write_ok` | Total successful writes across all ports. |
   112	| `write_full` | Total full-write attempts (queue had no space). |
   113	| `q_head` / `q_tail` | Shared-memory queue counters for the stalling port. `q_tail` = elements pushed by the producer; `q_head` = elements popped by the consumer. `q_head == q_tail` means the queue is empty. |
   114	
   115	### Enabling verbose per-element logging
   116	
   117	Set the `FRT_STREAM_DEBUG` environment variable to log every successful stream read and write:
   118	
   119	```bash
   120	FRT_STREAM_DEBUG=1 ./vadd --bitstream=vadd.xo 1000
   121	```
   122	
   123	### Interpreting stall patterns
   124	
   125	- **`q_tail=0`** on a consumer port: the producer never wrote to this stream. Check that the producer's xsim started and that stream arguments are bound correctly.
   126	- **`q_head == q_tail` but `read_ok < expected`**: all produced elements were consumed but not enough were produced. The producer may have exited before flushing all writes.
   127	- **`write_full` growing**: the consumer is not draining fast enough. Check for deadlocks or increase `TAPA_CONCURRENCY`.
   128	
   129	---
   130	
   131	```admonish tip
   132	Always pass software simulation before running fast cosim. Software simulation runs faster and catches logic bugs in C++. Fast cosim catches RTL bugs introduced by synthesis and scheduling. Skipping software simulation wastes cosim time on bugs that are much faster to fix at the C++ level.
   133	```
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	**See also:** [Common Errors](common-errors.md) | [Deadlocks & Hangs](deadlocks-and-hangs.md)

    75	---
    76	
    77	## Cosim produces wrong output (`FAIL!`) but xsim does not hang
    78	
    79	Run with waveform capture and a persistent work directory so you can inspect the simulation after it completes:
    80	
    81	```bash
    82	./vadd --bitstream=vadd.xo \
    83	  -cosim_work_dir ./cosim_work \
    84	  -xsim_save_waveform \
    85	  1000
    86	```
    87	
    88	Then open the waveform in Vivado GUI:
    89	
    90	```bash
    91	vivado -mode gui -source ./cosim_work/output/run/run_cosim.tcl
    92	```
    93	
    94	In the waveform viewer, add the AXI memory interface signals and compare the expected vs actual data on each transaction. Look for read data that does not match what the host wrote, or write transactions that target unexpected addresses.
    95	
    96	---
    97	
    98	## Stream diagnostics
    99	
   100	The DPI runtime reports stream progress periodically when a stream stalls (empty on read or full on write). These messages appear on stderr and include the port name and queue state:
   101	
   102	```
   103	frt-dpi: progress[a_fifo_s]: read_ok=16 read_empty=40M write_ok=0 write_full=0 q_head=8 q_tail=8
   104	```
   105	
   106	| Field | Meaning |
   107	|-------|---------|
   108	| `progress[port]` | The port that triggered the report (the one currently stalling). |
   109	| `read_ok` | Total successful reads across all ports in this process. |
   110	| `read_empty` | Total empty-read attempts (queue had no data). |
   111	| `write_ok` | Total successful writes across all ports. |
   112	| `write_full` | Total full-write attempts (queue had no space). |
   113	| `q_head` / `q_tail` | Shared-memory queue counters for the stalling port. `q_tail` = elements pushed by the producer; `q_head` = elements popped by the consumer. `q_head == q_tail` means the queue is empty. |
   114	
   115	### Enabling verbose per-element logging
   116	
   117	Set the `FRT_STREAM_DEBUG` environment variable to log every successful stream read and write:
   118	
   119	```bash
   120	FRT_STREAM_DEBUG=1 ./vadd --bitstream=vadd.xo 1000
   121	```
   122	
   123	### Interpreting stall patterns
   124	
   125	- **`q_tail=0`** on a consumer port: the producer never wrote to this stream. Check that the producer's xsim started and that stream arguments are bound correctly.
   126	- **`q_head == q_tail` but `read_ok < expected`**: all produced elements were consumed but not enough were produced. The producer may have exited before flushing all writes.
   127	- **`write_full` growing**: the consumer is not draining fast enough. Check for deadlocks or increase `TAPA_CONCURRENCY`.
   128	
   129	---
   130	
   131	```admonish tip
   132	Always pass software simulation before running fast cosim. Software simulation runs faster and catches logic bugs in C++. Fast cosim catches RTL bugs introduced by synthesis and scheduling. Skipping software simulation wastes cosim time on bugs that are much faster to fix at the C++ level.
   133	```
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	**See also:** [Common Errors](common-errors.md) | [Deadlocks & Hangs](deadlocks-and-hangs.md)
